candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 23 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 24 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 25 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 26 not required. 27
candidates.context: This document is intended to provide recommendations to sponsors and clinical investigators 14 developing early-phase trials, which include first-in-human (FIH) protocols or protocols for 15 drugs and biologic products 2 with limited human experience, submitted under an Investigational 16 New Drug Application (IND) to the appropriate disease-specific division located within the 17 Center for Drug Evaluation and Research’s Office of Oncologic Diseases (CDER/OOD) 3 and the 18 Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research’s Office of Clinical Evaluation (CBER/OCE) 4 . 19 This guidance is specific to solid tumors and does not address protocols for investigational drugs 20 intended to treat hematologic malignancies. 21

candidates.statement: Unnecessarily restrictive eligibility criteria may slow patient accrual, limit patient access to 47 early-phase trials, and lead to trial results that have limited applicability in the patient population 48 that will ultimately use the drug. Sponsors should reference FDA eligibility criteria guidances for 49 trials enrolling patients with cancer for additional early-phase trial considerations to ensure 50 patient safety and to ensure that access to clinical trials is not unnecessarily restricted. Many of 51 these guidances are cited in this section. 52
candidates.context: A. Eligibility Criteria 45

candidates.statement: • Eligibility criteria should include the requirement that patients have received available 56 therapy(ies) that offer the potential for cure, or such available therapy be administered to all 57 patients in the trial, where the investigational drug is added to such therapy (i.e., add-on 58 trial). 59 • When conducting clinical trials in a non-curative setting, patients may be eligible for 60 inclusion in trials, including early-phase trials, regardless of whether they have received 61 available therapy in the non-curative setting. 62 • Sponsors must ensure the elements of informed consent, as required by 21 CFR 50.25, are 63 addressed, including “a disclosure of appropriate alternative procedures or courses of 64 treatment, if any, that might be advantageous to the subject.” The informed consent must 65 clearly state whether other treatment options known to confer clinical benefit exist and must 66 include discussion of reasonably foreseeable risks and any potential benefits associated with 67 the administration of investigational drug. For disease settings in which there are available 68 therapies that have demonstrated prolongation in survival (i.e., an overall survival benefit), 69 these therapies should be explicitly stated in the informed consent document by name. 70

candidates.statement: Thoughtful consideration should be given to the potential inclusion of patients infected with 118 human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), and hepatitis C virus (HCV) in 119 cancer clinical trials. Eligibility criteria that address requirements regarding relevant concurrent 120 antiviral and other therapies (e.g., antibiotic prophylaxis) and degree of immunocompetence in 121 patients with HIV, HBV, or HCV infections should be designed in a manner that is appropriate 122 for a given cancer, investigational drug (for instance taking into account immunosuppressive 123 potential, drug-drug interaction, etc.), and intended use population. Inclusion of these patients in 124 early phase cancer clinical trials allows for evaluation of safe and effective use of the product 125 across a broader patient population likely to use the drug in clinical practice. 126

candidates.statement: • For a FIH trial, the primary objective(s) should be assessments of safety and tolerability. 193 • Other objectives can be secondary or exploratory and can include dose identification, 194 pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, immunogenicity (if applicable), biomarker analyses, 195 dose-exposure-response relationships, food effect/drug-drug interactions (if applicable), and 196 preliminary measures of activity (e.g., response rate). 197
candidates.context: 2. Dose Escalation Methods and Procedures 199

candidates.statement: • A rule-based or model-based design should be prespecified to guide the decisions regarding 203 the dosage of the investigational agent in subsequent cohorts to ensure adequate control of 204 the rate of excessive toxicity and the selection of a safe dose for further investigation. 205 • For dose escalation designs using decision criteria based on data from a single dose level 206 (e.g., Bayesian Optimal Interval [BOIN] design), ensure that the upper boundary allowing a 207 dose retention decision is specified and does not lead to an excessive observed toxicity rate. 208 • For dose escalation designs using decision rules based on data across all dose levels for 209 which a decision table cannot be pre-tabulated (e.g., Bayesian Logistic Regression Model 210 [BLRM]), a description of the data that support the assumptions for the model should be 211 provided and simulation studies should be conducted to evaluate the operating 212 characteristics of the design. The simulation studies should demonstrate a low probability of 213 selecting a dose with excessive toxicity and a low percentage of patients exposed to an 214 excessively toxic dose. The operating characteristics should be evaluated for robustness with 215 different parameter settings which violate the model assumptions. 216

candidates.statement: • IPDE should occur only if ≤ Grade 2 toxicity was observed during the previous treatment 235 cycle. 236 • The decision to allow for IPDE should be made after considering the potential safety profile 237 of the investigational drug, including cumulative drug toxicity. The maximal intra-patient 238 dose escalation level should only be at the highest cleared dose level. 239 • IPDE may not be suitable for certain drugs depending on their mechanism of action. For 240 example, because tumor burden differs between patients, a given dose that may be safe in 241 one patient with lower tumor burden may cause considerable toxicities at the same dose in 242 patients with higher tumor burden. 243

candidates.statement: • In general, the maximum dose increment for small molecules and ADCs should not exceed 247 100% and for biologics (with exception of ADCs) should not exceed half-log. Alternative 248 proposals should have adequate justification. 249 • Dose increments of less than 100% (e.g., modified Fibonacci or 50%) for small molecules 250 and ADCs, or less than half-log for biologics (with exception of ADCs and T-cell engagers 251 [TCE]) may be warranted if the following situations occur: 252 o If at least two ≥ Grade 2 treatment -emergent adverse events (TEAE) or one dose- 253 limiting toxicity (DLT) are observed across the cohort with at least three patients 254 enrolled. 255 o If a single ≥ Grade 2 adverse event occurs in a single patient cohort. The protocol 256 should be modified to require expansion of single patient cohorts (e.g., minimum 3 257 patients per cohort) for any ≥ Grade 2 adverse event, regardless of attribution. 258 • For TCE, dose increments should be limited to 100% or less for both step-up and full 259 treatment doses if one or more incidences of ≥ Grade 2 cytokine release syndrome (CRS) 260 during the DLT period and to 50% or less if two or more incidences of ≥ Grade 2 CRS or one 261 or more DLT is observed during the DLT period. Optimize the step-up dosing regimen (e.g., 262 step-up dose(s) and dosing schedule) that can minimize the risk of ≥ Grade 3 CRS. 263

candidates.statement: • For first-in-human trials, investigational drug(s) may have certain serious expected toxicities 267 based on non-clinical studies, existing human data, or both on similar products. Depending 268 on the expected toxicities and their severity, dosing several patients simultaneously may 269 represent an unreasonable risk. To address this issue, sponsors may need to provide a plan to 270 stagger administering the product to successive patients to limit the number of patients who 271 might be exposed to risk within a cohort, followed by staggering between cohorts. The plan 272 to stagger patients should include: 273 o Justification showing that the interval is long enough to monitor for acute and 274 subacute events 275 o Consideration of the time course of adverse events that were observed in animal 276 studies and in previous human experience with related products 277 o Consideration of the expected duration of the drug’s activity 278

candidates.statement: The recommended approach for early-phase trials is typically a modified fasted condition (such 468 as taking on an empty stomach, defined as at least 1 hour before and 2 hours after a meal). This 469 approach avoids confounding dose-finding assessments while maintaining patient safety and 470 tolerability. Alternative food intake instructions may be supported with adequate justifications, 471 such as anticipated gastrointestinal intolerability. If the investigational drug is to be administered 472 with food, protocols should provide adequate PK and safety justification and detailed meal 473 composition. In subsequent trials, food administration requirements may be modified based on 474 emerging pharmacokinetic and safety data, including results from preliminary or dedicated food 475 effect studies. 476

candidates.statement: Protocols should include pharmacokinetic (PK) sampling plans that adequately characterize the 482 PK profile of the investigational drug and support dosage selection for subsequent trials. The 483 sampling plan should clearly specify which analyte or analytes will be measured. 484
candidates.context: For early-phase trials, FDA recommends including intensive PK sampling following the first 486 dose and at steady state or after multiple doses. Additionally, it is recommended to include 487 sparse sampling throughout the study to support population pharmacokinetic modeling and 488 exposure-response analyses. The sampling plan should include samples around the anticipated 489 time of the maximum concentration, if applicable and extend sufficiently to characterize the 490 elimination phase, with the duration informed by the anticipated elimination half-life based on 491 nonclinical data or data from related compounds. In subsequent trials, PK sampling frequency 492 and timing may be adjusted based on emerging pharmacokinetic and safety data. 493
